lines.text: towards new ideals and goals. His word spells a radical
challenge to the world's very existence and way of life; His
word challenges the world with regard to its meaning and
justification; indeed, it accuses the world of imagining that
it possesses in itself independent meaning and justification;
it accuses the world of having gone astray through the dream
of its independence and self-sufficiency, and it calls the world
back from the sphere of the visible to that of the invisible.
Thus Jesus does not move in the world as belonging to it, but He
confronts it as the One who wills to save it from the illusion
of its self-sufficiency and who for that reason must be its accuser.
The word "world" here does not mean the world of nature,
nor the world as the field of possibilities, gifts and tasks for
human thinking and creative effort. "World" here is not the
world as the creation of God, but "world" in a quite specific
sense, i.e. the world in so far as it stands under the control
of the "prince of this world". The "prince of this world" is
the peculiar domination which this world of possibilities,
gifts and tasks can achieve and exercise over the minds of
men. Whoever surrenders himself to it experiences this
peculiar domination which aspires to master him, which
gains a tyrannous hold of him in work, in pleasure and in
pain, with the result that his whole outlook, his thoughts
and desires are fettered and can no longer gain freedom from
this tyranny.
We must not deceive ourselves. It is not here a question
of the so-called world which tempts man astray into the
so-called paths of evil, into bad immoral actions. No, the
world exercises its tyrannous sway precisely as much over
moral men as over immoral men, and it must never be
forgotten that the struggle of Jesus against the world was
precisely a struggle against very earnestly moral men. "All
things are lawful for me"
, says Paul (1 Cor. 6: 12), "but I will
not be enslaved by anything." And the characteristic
dominion and sway exercised by the world is to enslave men
in good as well as in evil, in the pedestrian work of every day
as in the most exalted strivings, in pleasures as in struggles to
attain the highest ends:
